issue.body_html:
On Android OS, the list of Root Certificates loaded by the DartSDK SecurityContext is loaded from the directory /system/etc/security/cacerts.

The Root Certificate files placed in this path will match the System Certificates in the Trusted credentials on the Android OS.

However, even if Certificate is set to Disable on the Android OS, the Root Certificate file will not be removed from /system/etc/security/cacerts. So even if a user sets any Root Certificate to be untrusted, the DartSDK will ignore that setting and trust it.

Steps to reproduce:

  1. On AndroidOS, disable the System Root Certificate DigiCert High Assurance EV Root CA in Trusted credentials.
  2. Using the http package of DartSDK, connect to the server where DigiCert High Assurance EV Root CA will be the RootCA. An example of the code is shown below.
dart
// RootCA for www.intellilink.co.jp FQDN is DigiCert High Assurance EV Root CA
http.get(Uri.parse('https://www.intellilink.co.jp'));
  1. For the reasons explained above, DartSDK trusts the Root Certificate with the disabled setting and establishes communication with it. Note that NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID is generated when you connect to https://www.intellilink.co.jp with Google Chrome, which confirms that the above disabled setting is working.

issue.body:
On Android OS, the list of Root Certificates loaded by the DartSDK SecurityContext is loaded from the directory /system/etc/security/cacerts.

The Root Certificate files placed in this path will match the System Certificates in the Trusted credentials on the Android OS. 

However, even if Certificate is set to Disable on the Android OS, the Root Certificate file will not be removed from /system/etc/security/cacerts. So even if a user sets any Root Certificate to be untrusted, the DartSDK will ignore that setting and trust it.

Steps to reproduce:

1. On AndroidOS, disable the System Root Certificate DigiCert High Assurance EV Root CA in Trusted credentials.
2. Using the `http` package of DartSDK, connect to the server where DigiCert High Assurance EV Root CA will be the RootCA. An example of the code is shown below.
```
dart
// RootCA for www.intellilink.co.jp FQDN is DigiCert High Assurance EV Root CA
http.get(Uri.parse('https://www.intellilink.co.jp'));
```
3. For the reasons explained above, DartSDK trusts the Root Certificate with the disabled setting and establishes communication with it. Note that NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID is generated when you connect to https://www.intellilink.co.jp with Google Chrome, which confirms that the above disabled setting is working.

comments.body_html:
@acoutts
Yes, many corporate Wifi network setups will not work with Dart/Flutter (at least with Android devices).
In one app, we've built a workaround where a required certificate would be installed into the app per MDM additionally to installing it in the OS itself.
That is brittle workaround, though.

We've also tried to pipe all traffic not through dart.http but wrote native plugin code for that instead. This will fail for everything that you don't control directly, though, like image loading or video streaming.

In the end, we scrapped the Flutter project for all business apps, and started re-implementing natively.

I wish Flutter/Dart would put a clear warning on their pages, like: Corporate networks are not supported.

Hey @komaxx,

I'd like to understand your use case (and I'm not familiar with how typical corporate networks do security).

So the corporate network that you are trying to access requires a client certificate. When you were explicitly setting the certificate in your app, were you using SecurityContext.useCertificateChainBytes?

Would [getCertificateChain](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain#getCertificateChain(android.content.Context,%20java.lang.String) have provided the certificate that you needed?

What did your native plugin do? Provide the needed certificate, do the entire HTTP transport or something else?

Thanks for your help!

Could this also mean if a user has explicitly added a new certificate to their system, dart wouldn't trust it?

It depends on how and kind of a certificate was added to the system.
Generally speaking, by default dart app will pick up trusted_root_certs from the system, so if a user adds new new trusted root cert to the system, dart app will use it. Dart developer can also allows force use of trusted roots certs that are built-in into the dart vm(via SecurityContext(withTrustedRoots:true)). Dart developer can also explicitly specify certificates that should be used(via SecurityContext.setTrustedCertificates

I recommend opening new issue for the issue you see, since this one is specifically about handling of disabled certs on Android, and providing more details along the lines @brianquinlan suggested.

comments.body_html:
Hi @brianquinlan

Happy to help!
Here's what I've encountered as a common corporate network setup: (Android) devices are controlled via some sort of MDM (Knox, MobileIron, ..). Via these MDMs, self-signed certificates are installed on the phones. In the settings app on the phone, these will then show up as user-added certificates.
Also Wifi connections are often set-up to use a man-in-the-middle proxy (for "security") which uses again a self-signed certificate for TLS.

For the browser, everything works then out-of-the-box: Browser apps by default trust user-added certificates.

For native Android apps, there is only a small change necessary: One just has to add a security config XML file that enables user-installed certificates as trust-anchors (see: https://developer.android.com/training/articles/security-config). Proxy settings are honored automatically.

For Flutter apps, we're now in hot water:

  • First, Flutter will not respect the phones proxy settings (see: flutter/flutter#26359)
  • Then, when a workaround for that was made, the user-installed certificates will not be accepted. For this, we could not find a simple solution, as there seems to be no easy way to read user-certificates from the system.

With one customer we could build a scheme where the PEM of the used self-signed certificate would be transported to the app via MDM. Then, we simply registered an HttpOverride and created a HttpClient that would check in its badCertificateCallback against this pem. It works - but it puts our app at a disadvantage against competitor's apps that don't need fiddling around with certificates in MDM interfaces.

The second workaround was to simply dump all http requesting into a plugin and run the requests natively. That gets old quickly (multipart requets, custom headers, error handling, ..) as we had to re-implement parts of the http interface, but it works - for http requests that we do ourself; implicit requests (e.g. Image.network) fail. One can write workarounds for all those things as well. However, we decided at that point to go for a different platform for apps targeted at corporate customers.

Would [getCertificateChain](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain#getCertificateChain(android.content.Context,%20java.lang.String) have provided the certificate that you needed?

I don't know :/ This did not turn up in my research at the time, and right now I don't know how I would use it, sorry!

I hope that makes things a bit clearer?

Security impact: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise (October 2026)

Hi Dart team,

I'd like to raise a security-related concern in connection with this issue, following the recent eMudhra intermediate CA private key compromise, disclosed on October 20, 2026.

Incident details:
https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

Eight intermediate CA private keys were compromised, potentially allowing attackers to impersonate HTTPS services.

Major browsers and operating systems have deployed mitigations through certificate revocation or blocklists. However, some non-browser TLS clients may remain vulnerable because they do not enforce these mechanisms.

Potential impact on Dart/Flutter for Android

As described in this issue, Dart's SecurityContext on Android loads trusted CA certificates from /system/etc/security/cacerts, rather than fully relying on Android's platform trust evaluation.

This raises a related concern:

Does Dart's HttpClient honor Android's certificate revocation and blocklist mechanisms, including the mitigations deployed for the compromised eMudhra intermediates?

Even if Android has blocked these certificates, Dart applications using dart:io might still accept certificate chains involving the compromised intermediates if the relevant revocation or blocklist checks are not enforced.

Questions

  1. Does dart:io / HttpClient on Android honor certificate revocation and blocklists distributed through Android platform security updates or Google Play services?

  2. Are the compromised eMudhra intermediate CA certificates currently rejected by Dart's TLS implementation on Android?

  3. Does the behavior differ between Android, iOS, and macOS, particularly where platform-native trust evaluation is used?

  4. If Dart is affected, is a Dart SDK security update planned, or is there a recommended mitigation for Flutter applications?

Reproduction / verification

The incident disclosure provides public TLS test endpoints:

  • https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/
  • https://dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

These can be tested using Dart's standard HttpClient, without disabling certificate verification.

Successful TLS negotiation with a compromised certificate chain would indicate a potential security issue requiring further investigation.

I have not yet independently confirmed whether current Dart/Flutter versions accept these chains on Android.

Given the potential impact on Flutter applications handling authentication tokens, API credentials, and sensitive user data, an official assessment of Dart's TLS behavior would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you!

Major browsers and operating systems have deployed mitigations through certificate revocation or blocklists. However, some non-browser TLS clients may remain vulnerable because they do not enforce these mechanisms.

### Potential impact on Dart/Flutter for Android

As described in this issue, Dart's `SecurityContext` on Android loads trusted CA certificates from `/system/etc/security/cacerts`, rather than fully relying on Android's platform trust evaluation.

This raises a related concern:

### Questions

timeline.body_html:
Hi @brianquinlan

Happy to help!
Here's what I've encountered as a common corporate network setup: (Android) devices are controlled via some sort of MDM (Knox, MobileIron, ..). Via these MDMs, self-signed certificates are installed on the phones. In the settings app on the phone, these will then show up as user-added certificates.
Also Wifi connections are often set-up to use a man-in-the-middle proxy (for "security") which uses again a self-signed certificate for TLS.

For the browser, everything works then out-of-the-box: Browser apps by default trust user-added certificates.

For native Android apps, there is only a small change necessary: One just has to add a security config XML file that enables user-installed certificates as trust-anchors (see: https://developer.android.com/training/articles/security-config). Proxy settings are honored automatically.

For Flutter apps, we're now in hot water:

  • First, Flutter will not respect the phones proxy settings (see: flutter/flutter#26359)
  • Then, when a workaround for that was made, the user-installed certificates will not be accepted. For this, we could not find a simple solution, as there seems to be no easy way to read user-certificates from the system.

With one customer we could build a scheme where the PEM of the used self-signed certificate would be transported to the app via MDM. Then, we simply registered an HttpOverride and created a HttpClient that would check in its badCertificateCallback against this pem. It works - but it puts our app at a disadvantage against competitor's apps that don't need fiddling around with certificates in MDM interfaces.

The second workaround was to simply dump all http requesting into a plugin and run the requests natively. That gets old quickly (multipart requets, custom headers, error handling, ..) as we had to re-implement parts of the http interface, but it works - for http requests that we do ourself; implicit requests (e.g. Image.network) fail. One can write workarounds for all those things as well. However, we decided at that point to go for a different platform for apps targeted at corporate customers.

Would [getCertificateChain](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/security/KeyChain#getCertificateChain(android.content.Context,%20java.lang.String) have provided the certificate that you needed?

I don't know :/ This did not turn up in my research at the time, and right now I don't know how I would use it, sorry!

I hope that makes things a bit clearer?

timeline.body_html:
Security impact: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise (October 2026)

Hi Dart team,

I'd like to raise a security-related concern in connection with this issue, following the recent eMudhra intermediate CA private key compromise, disclosed on October 20, 2026.

Incident details:
https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

Eight intermediate CA private keys were compromised, potentially allowing attackers to impersonate HTTPS services.

Major browsers and operating systems have deployed mitigations through certificate revocation or blocklists. However, some non-browser TLS clients may remain vulnerable because they do not enforce these mechanisms.

Potential impact on Dart/Flutter for Android

As described in this issue, Dart's SecurityContext on Android loads trusted CA certificates from /system/etc/security/cacerts, rather than fully relying on Android's platform trust evaluation.

This raises a related concern:

Does Dart's HttpClient honor Android's certificate revocation and blocklist mechanisms, including the mitigations deployed for the compromised eMudhra intermediates?

Even if Android has blocked these certificates, Dart applications using dart:io might still accept certificate chains involving the compromised intermediates if the relevant revocation or blocklist checks are not enforced.

Questions

  1. Does dart:io / HttpClient on Android honor certificate revocation and blocklists distributed through Android platform security updates or Google Play services?

  2. Are the compromised eMudhra intermediate CA certificates currently rejected by Dart's TLS implementation on Android?

  3. Does the behavior differ between Android, iOS, and macOS, particularly where platform-native trust evaluation is used?

  4. If Dart is affected, is a Dart SDK security update planned, or is there a recommended mitigation for Flutter applications?

Reproduction / verification

The incident disclosure provides public TLS test endpoints:

  • https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/
  • https://dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

These can be tested using Dart's standard HttpClient, without disabling certificate verification.

Successful TLS negotiation with a compromised certificate chain would indicate a potential security issue requiring further investigation.

I have not yet independently confirmed whether current Dart/Flutter versions accept these chains on Android.

Given the potential impact on Flutter applications handling authentication tokens, API credentials, and sensitive user data, an official assessment of Dart's TLS behavior would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you!
